I am particularly fascinated with WhatsApp because of its versatility and agility as far as social media platforms are concerned. It takes customer privacy and security into great context and go out of their way to protect that customer information from 3rd parties and hackers. I have never heard of a hack or security breach into WhatsApp security systems. Overall the App has been great and has eased the way the world has connected via talking and sharing digital and graphical data. 

The only downside to WhatsApp is that when you lose your device or are out of storage and uninstall the app, you typically lose all your previous chats and data. I would have been great if WhatsApp had an option for optional storage space for sale, for folk to backup their communication and social media data. 

Thank you

WhatsApp was what I used when I studied abroad to communicate with friends and family, but I unfortunately the app has so many issues that I refuse to use it even if that means it will be more difficult to communicate with those same friends and family living abroad. The app does provide some privacy in messaging, but based on the updated service agreements, it seems clear that Meta plans to use and train large language models on private messages. Additionally, WhatsApp has a series of issues regarding collecting metadata of its users and having nearly total freedom to monetize that information. I hate the idea of an app that claims to provide private and secure communication that is simultaneously monetizing my data.

The app is also filled with scammers. I receive near daily notifications from massive cryptocurrency scam groups adding me to group chats promising “massive returns on my investment.” No matter how many times I report these groups, they just keep popping up. I blame the extraction of all contacts from your phone that WhatsApp uses to help you communicate with others through the app. It’s clear that Meta is doing nothing to address these issues and they continue to violate our data while doing nothing.

If I could go back and never use the app in the first place, I would do it in a heartbeat. There other options for communication with family and friends abroad that does not come with the same issues that WhatsApp promises.

Zuckerberg and his team have built an empire on the backs of people’s privacy violations, all for the sake of profit. WhatsApp has become more about exploiting its users than providing any kind of meaningful communication. If you're still using WhatsApp, you're essentially handing over your life for free—while Zuckerberg and his company profit off of it. Do yourself a favor: delete your account and find a platform that values your privacy. WhatsApp is a data thief, plain and simple.

I used to love WhatsApp it was a reliable, straightforward messaging app, but ever since Meta acquired it, it’s become a privacy nightmare. The app is now riddled with issues that never existed before: intrusive data-sharing practices with Facebook, annoying prompts to link your account to Facebook services, and the feeling that Meta is constantly mining your personal data for advertising purposes. The end-to-end encryption, which was once the app's selling point, now feels like a hollow promise when you know your data is still being tracked and sold.

The user experience has also declined. Updates seem to focus more on adding features no one asked for, like status updates and business profiles, rather than fixing bugs or improving performance. The app is often slow and crashes unexpectedly. There’s also a growing number of ads disguised as "business messages," and the once-simple interface now feels bloated and cluttered.

Since Meta took over, WhatsApp no longer feels like a trustworthy, secure way to communicate. It’s clear that privacy is no longer a priority, and the constant data harvesting makes this app hard to recommend. Look elsewhere if you care about your privacy.

During my recent travel to a foreign country, WhatsApp shockingly suspended my phone number without any valid explanation. As we're aware, in many parts of Europe and Latin America, businesses rely heavily on WhatsApp for customer communication. In fact, I was explicitly advised by the hotels in Peru to use WhatsApp as the primary means of contact during my stay.

Right in the midst of providing crucial information to the hotel for my pickup arrangement, WhatsApp abruptly disabled my number. I promptly submitted a review request to reinstate my number, but to my utter dismay, WhatsApp not only failed to address the issue but completely banned my number!

I found myself stranded in the remote mountains of Peru, desperately needing to contact the hotel for pickup. Unfortunately, the hotel didn't answer my phone calls, and I couldn't communicate in the local language. To make matters worse, this happened just as the sun was setting. The timing of WhatsApp's arbitrary number suspension couldn't have been more disastrous, leaving me in a state of extreme distress with no means of reaching the hotel.

WhatsApp used to be my go-to messaging app, but over time, it has become increasingly unreliable and frustrating. One of the biggest issues is the constant syncing problems—sometimes messages just don’t come through, and you have to manually refresh or restart the app. The notifications are often delayed, and I’ve missed important messages because of it. 

The app also feels bloated with unnecessary features like status updates, which I never use, but seem to take up space in the interface. The lack of customization options is another drawback—you're stuck with a generic chat layout and minimal control over how the app looks or works.

The privacy concerns have also grown significantly. The integration with Facebook (now Meta) feels like a major step backward, and it's unclear how much of your data is being shared or tracked across platforms. It’s hard to trust an app that constantly seems to prioritize corporate interests over user privacy.

Additionally, video and voice calls often suffer from poor quality, especially on weaker connections, and it’s still prone to crashing or freezing, making basic functions unreliable. Overall, it’s disappointing how an app that was once simple and effective has now become bogged down with bugs, ads, and questionable privacy practices.

When I first started using WhatsApp, it was a straightforward, secure, and ad-free way to communicate with friends and family around the world. The focus was on privacy and simplicity—everything you’d want in a messaging app. But since Meta took over, the experience has steadily declined.

The app now feels less about connection and more about monetization. Meta’s creeping data practices, combined with their attempts to push features like business accounts and integrations, have made WhatsApp feel less private and more like another way for Meta to profit off its users. Even with claims of end-to-end encryption, it’s hard to trust a company that has consistently prioritized engagement and profit over transparency.

Like Facebook and Instagram, WhatsApp is now tied to Meta’s broader ecosystem of divisive politics and misinformation. The platform has also become a breeding ground for fake news, amplified by Zuckerberg’s recent decision to stop fact-checking certain types of content. It’s troubling to see a platform once known for secure and simple communication become another channel for unchecked propaganda and poorly targeted ads.

WhatsApp used to be a reliable and trusted messaging app. Now, it’s just another cog in Meta’s machine, and it’s no longer worth using if you value your privacy and sanity. Disappointing.

WhatsApp markets itself as a “secure” messaging app, but don’t be fooled. While its end-to-end encryption is solid, the app collects a shocking amount of personal data behind the scenes. It gathers information about your contacts, location, device usage, and even your interactions within the app—all of which is shared with its parent company, Meta (Facebook). This happens with little transparency and often without real consent.

The privacy policy is vague and filled with legal jargon, making it nearly impossible to understand exactly what you’re agreeing to. Meta’s history of data misuse only adds to the distrust. For an app that claims to prioritize privacy, this level of data collection feels like a complete betrayal.

Beyond privacy concerns, the app is riddled with annoying issues. It’s constantly nagging you to back up your chats to the cloud, which isn’t encrypted, leaving your data vulnerable. The interface feels outdated, and updates often introduce more bugs than fixes.

If you value your privacy or want to avoid being a pawn in Meta’s endless data-harvesting schemes, it’s time to switch to a messaging app that actually respects you.

WhatsApp markets itself as a secure, encrypted messaging platform, but its ownership by Meta casts a shadow over its privacy claims. Despite promises of end-to-end encryption, the app still collects metadata—information about who you message, how often, and when. This metadata is valuable to advertisers and can be used to build detailed user profiles. The controversial update to its privacy policy in 2021, which allowed more data sharing with Facebook, highlighted Meta’s true intentions. As a dominant player in the messaging space, WhatsApp leaves users with few alternatives, cementing Meta’s monopoly in digital communication.

To turn on previews that display both the contact name and message:

Go to WhatsApp > Settings > Notifications > turn Show Previewon. 
Go to iPhone Settings > Notifications > WhatsApp > Show Previews > Always (Default) or When Unlocked.
To turn on previews that display the contact name but not message:

Go to WhatsApp > Settings > Notifications > turn Show Previewon. 
Go to iPhone Settings > Notifications > WhatsApp > Show Previews > Never.
